# The Decoyed Object of Desire

## The Fort He Wanted Destroyed

It's 1711 and the Duke of Marlborough has a problem with a French fort.

The fort protects a road he needs. He wants it gone. But he can't destroy it himself — the moment he does, the French will understand that he wants to march down that road, and they'll prepare accordingly.[^1]

So he captures the fort and puts his own troops in it. Occupies it. Holds it. Makes it look like the fort matters to him for some purpose of his own.

The French attack. He lets them take it back.

And having retaken it, they demolish it — because obviously the duke had wanted it for some important reason, and they weren't going to leave him a second chance.[^1]

The road is now unprotected. Marlborough marches into France.

He got his enemy to do the work, for free, and to feel clever about it.

## The Premise: Why Openness Loses

Before the technique, Greene lays out why anyone would need it, and the argument is blunter than people expect.

> *Most people are open books. They say what they feel, blurt out their opinions at every opportunity, and constantly reveal their plans and intentions.*[^2]

Two reasons, he says. It's easy and natural — controlling your tongue takes effort. And many people believe openness wins hearts and shows good nature.

> *They are greatly deluded. Honesty is actually a blunt instrument, which bloodies more than it cuts.*[^2]

Then the claim that actually carries the law, which is about status rather than safety:

> *by being unabashedly open you make yourself so predictable and familiar that it is almost impossible to respect or fear you, and power will not accrue to a person who cannot inspire such emotions.*[^2]

That's worth separating from the tactical argument. Concealment isn't only about stopping people countering you. It's that **legibility itself is low-status** — a person whose next move can be predicted is a person who has stopped being interesting, and Greene treats interest as the raw material of power.

## The Mechanism: First Instinct Is to Trust Appearances

The technique rests on one stated fact about people:

> *Our first instinct is to always trust appearances. We cannot go around doubting the reality of what we see and hear—constantly imagining that appearances concealed something else would exhaust and terrify us.*[^3]

This is a good argument and it's doing real work. Scepticism isn't free. Treating every visible thing as potentially staged is metabolically expensive and, past a point, indistinguishable from paranoia. So people default to belief, not from stupidity but from budget.

Which makes the decoy cheap to run:

> *Simply dangle an object you seem to desire, a goal you seem to aim for, in front of people's eyes and they will take the appearance for reality. Once their eyes focus on the decoy, they will fail to notice what you are really up to.*[^3]

## Analytical Case Study: Why Marlborough's Version Is the Strong Form

Most decoys just misdirect attention. Marlborough's does something better, and the difference is worth isolating.

A plain decoy costs you effort and buys you a distraction. You appear to want X, the enemy watches X, you take Y. Fine — but you're still doing all the work on Y yourself.

Marlborough converted the enemy's counter-move into his own objective.

Run the chain. He wants the fort gone. He can't destroy it without revealing the road matters. So he makes the fort itself look valuable — and the French, reasoning correctly from what they observe, conclude that anything Marlborough values should be denied to him.

**They demolish it.** Their most rational defensive act is the thing he needed done.

That's the strong form: not *look elsewhere while I act*, but *let me arrange things so your best counter-move is my objective*. The enemy isn't merely deceived, they're **employed** — and they can't be talked out of it by anyone, because the reasoning is sound. Given what they could see, demolishing that fort was correct.

The vulnerability isn't in their judgement. It's in their inputs, and Greene's point is that inputs are the cheapest thing in the world to supply.

## Supporting a Cause You Detest

Greene names the highest-value version of the decoy, and it's the one Bismarck used:

> *A tactic that is often effective in setting up a red herring is to appear to support an idea or cause that is actually contrary to your own sentiments.*[^4]

Why it works:

> *Most people will believe you have experienced a change of heart, since it is so unusual to play so lightly with something as emotional as one's opinions and values.*[^4]

The load-bearing word is *unusual*. The technique runs on the rarity of its own use. People don't treat stated values as a possible manoeuvre because most people, most of the time, aren't manoeuvring with them — so the base rate protects the deceiver.

Which is a fragile foundation, and Greene doesn't say so. A technique that works because nobody expects it stops working exactly to the degree it becomes known.

## Talk More, Not Less

The counterintuitive instruction, and the most immediately usable thing in the law:

> *Hide your intentions not by closing up (with the risk of appearing secretive, and making people suspicious) but by talking endlessly about your desires and goals—just not your real ones.*[^5]

Greene's accounting: you kill three birds. You appear friendly, open and trusting. You conceal your intentions. And you send rivals on *"time-consuming wild-goose chases."*[^5]

Note the asymmetry in that third one. Silence costs your rival nothing — they simply learn nothing. A false goal costs them **weeks**, because they have to take it seriously, prepare against it, and allocate real resources.

Concealment by silence is defensive. Concealment by false disclosure is an attack that looks like candour.

## Implementation Workflow

You're going after something at work and there are two other people who'd want it if they knew it was available.

The instinct is to go quiet. Say nothing, move carefully, hope nobody notices.

Watch what silence actually does. You were talkative and now you're not, and the people who know you will register the change without being able to name it. You've told them something is happening and given them nothing to be wrong about — which is the worst of both.

So do the opposite, with one rule: the false goal has to be **real enough to cost you something.**

Not a lie. A genuine second interest you actually do have, talked about openly and often. The project you'd also enjoy. The skill you're also building. When someone asks what you're working toward, tell them that, and mean it, because you do.

Two things follow. Your rivals spend real attention on a thing that isn't the thing. And you're never caught in a falsehood, because everything you said was true — you simply declined to rank your interests out loud.

Then the Marlborough question, which is the one worth actually asking: **is there a version where their counter-move does my work?** If your rival, seeing you invest in that second area, would move to cover it — does their covering it clear something you need? Sometimes yes. Usually not. But it's the question that separates a distraction from a manoeuvre, and it costs nothing to ask.

## What This Costs

Greene doesn't price it, so here it is.

A person running this consistently is spending their credibility as an informant about themselves. Every time you describe your goals falsely — even by omission, even truthfully-but-misleadingly — you're drawing down a balance you can't see.

And the technique has no off switch. You cannot conceal your intentions from rivals and disclose them to allies, because the same room contains both and the categories move. Which means the practised version of this law produces someone whose stated goals are **structurally uninformative** to everybody, including the people they'd want to be known by.

Greene will spend Law 18 arguing that isolation is fatal. He does not connect it to this.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support.** Marlborough is a dated, specific military case with a clean causal chain and an outcome, and the mechanism generalises without strain. The premise about trusting appearances is argued from cognitive cost rather than asserted.

**Tension — the technique depends on being rare and the book is famous.** Greene's stated reason the change-of-heart decoy works is that playing lightly with values is *unusual*. A widely-read manual teaching that move erodes the base rate it runs on. Nothing in the law acknowledges that its own publication is a cost to its readers.

**Tension — against Part I's own opening.** Part I says all is lost if the target has *"the slightest suspicion."*[^6] But the recommended method is loud false disclosure, which invites scrutiny by design and survives it because the disclosed goal is real. Those are different theories of how deception survives contact.

**Tension — against Law 18.** *Do Not Build Fortresses to Protect Yourself — Isolation Is Dangerous.* Systematically misrepresenting your intentions to everyone around you is a route to exactly that isolation. Documented pair for the tension log.

🚩 SINGLE SOURCE · 🚩 SECONDARY WITHOUT PRIMARY — the Marlborough episode is undated beyond the year, unsourced, and the French reasoning is narrated from inside. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`.

**Open questions.**

- Marlborough's version requires predicting the enemy's counter-move precisely. How often is that available, and is the strong form actually rare enough to be a curiosity rather than a technique?
- If the decoy must be a genuine second interest to be safe, is this concealment at all — or just declining to rank?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Greene's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/deception-misdirection-tactics|Deception and Misdirection Tactics]], from the vault's Hughes corpus, works the same territory from an operator's manual rather than a historical one.

The two agree on the substrate — attention is single-channel, and occupying it is cheaper than defeating it — and split on the timescale.

The Hughes-style material is built for **an interaction**: minutes, a conversation, a room. Misdirection there is tactical and disposable, and it ends when the interaction does.

Greene's decoy runs for **months**, and that changes what it requires. A false goal you maintain across a year has to be resourced. Marlborough had to actually garrison the fort. Bismarck had to actually give the speech and live with having given it.

The pairing yields the cost curve neither states: **short-run misdirection is nearly free and long-run misdirection is an investment that must be genuinely funded** — which is why most people who try the second version fail at it. They deploy a conversational technique on a strategic timescale and are surprised when a decoy nobody was paying for stops convincing anyone.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**→ history · [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/sun-tzu-deception-and-formlessness|Sun-tzu on Deception and Formlessness]]**

The Chinese material, held in the vault from a scholarly source rather than a popular one, teaches appearing weak where strong and disordered where ordered — and Sun-tzu's frame is fundamentally about **shaping what the enemy believes about your state.**

Marlborough does something that frame doesn't contain, and the gap is instructive.

Sun-tzu's deceiver falsifies a *condition* and waits for the enemy to act on it. The enemy's error is the payoff. Marlborough falsifies a *preference* and the enemy's **correct** response is the payoff — the French did not blunder, they reasoned well from bad inputs and executed his plan.

That's a genuinely different operation. One exploits a misreading; the other exploits sound reasoning.

And it produces a defence neither source states. Against Sun-tzu's version, you defend by scouting — verify the condition independently and the deception fails. Against Marlborough's, scouting makes it *worse*, because better observation of the garrisoned fort only confirms that he values it. **The counter to a preference-decoy is not more information about what your opponent is doing. It's asking what your own best response would accomplish for them** — a question no reconnaissance can answer and almost nobody thinks to ask.

**→ business · [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/entertained-uncertainty-suspense-marketing|Entertained Uncertainty and Suspense Marketing]]**

The business page treats withheld information as a commercial asset: the unrevealed thing holds attention, and the reveal spends it.

Set against Greene's premise and the two halves of one economics appear.

Greene says openness destroys standing — *"by being unabashedly open you make yourself so predictable and familiar that it is almost impossible to respect or fear you."* The marketing page says the same about products, and has a mechanism for it: attention is sustained by an open loop and released by closing it.

Together they give the general form: **predictability is not a neutral property, it's a depreciating one.** Every fully disclosed intention closes a loop, and closed loops stop generating attention. That's why Greene's status argument and the suspense-marketing argument are the same argument at different scales.

But the pairing also exposes what Greene's version is missing. Marketing knows the loop must eventually close, and prices the reveal as the moment of conversion — the whole apparatus exists to be spent. Greene's law has no such moment. It teaches indefinite concealment with no account of what the withheld intention is ultimately *for*, which is the same structural gap that leaves Ninon's campaign unfinishable. **A technique borrowed from an economics of the reveal, run by someone who never intends to reveal, has quietly discarded the part that made it pay.**

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The strong form of this law isn't hiding what you want — it's arranging matters so that **your opponent's most rational move is the one you needed made.** Marlborough's French were not fooled about anything except which fort mattered, and from that single false input they reasoned flawlessly to his objective. Which means the real vulnerability in any adversary is never their judgement. It's the fact that you can often choose what they are reasoning about.

**Generative questions.**

- If the change-of-heart decoy works because value-manoeuvring is rare, what happens to it in an environment where everyone has read this book — does it invert into a tell?
- Greene's safest version of the decoy is a genuine second interest. Is there a meaningful line between strategic emphasis and deception, and does this law need one?
- The technique produces a person whose stated goals inform nobody. Law 18 says isolation kills. Is the practised concealer's isolation a side effect, or the price?

## Connected Concepts

# AI as Tyler Cowen Substitute — Generalist Sparring Partner

## A Tyler-Like Creature in His Pocket

Wang has a friend named Tyler. He sees Tyler maybe once every couple of months — drinks in DC, an afternoon in New York. In between visits, Wang keeps a running list of questions in his notes app: things he is wondering about, half-formed observations he wants Tyler's reaction to, intellectual loose ends. When the next visit comes, Wang shows up and *bombards him with a couple of things that I've been thinking,* and Tyler somehow expects this and absorbs it.[^1]

This Tyler is Tyler Cowen. Economics professor at George Mason. Author of an enormous corpus across economics, food, travel, philosophy, AI, culture. The kind of generalist who can give you a useful reaction to a Beethoven string quartet, a Stendhal novel, a Mongolian noodle, a Catholic theological dispute, a chess opening, and a forecast about the next decade of geopolitics — sometimes in the same conversation. The Tyler-experience for someone like Wang is the experience of having a *generalist sparring partner of unusual depth*, available occasionally, with whom rapid-fire intellectual exchange produces sharper thinking than the person could have produced alone.

Then ChatGPT arrived, and Wang noticed something odd about it.

The voice and the intellectual style of the model felt *familiar*.

## The Tyler-Influence Claim

Wang's claim is specific. *Tyler Cowen's thought has influenced a lot of how ChatGPT communicates*, and *this is on the record, I believe, and this is kind of established.*[^1] The claim refers to the well-known fact that Cowen's writing — across his blog *Marginal Revolution*, his books, his Bloomberg columns, his Conversations with Tyler podcast transcripts — is part of the publicly-available training corpus that LLMs learn on. Cowen has been extraordinarily prolific in public-facing prose for two decades, in a recognizable analytical voice that emphasizes economic reasoning, comparative observation, willingness to hold counterintuitive positions, and a particular kind of rapid-fire associative intelligence. That body of work has been absorbed into the training data of the major LLMs, and the models have learned, among many other things, *how Tyler Cowen thinks*.

The model is not Tyler Cowen. The model is a probabilistic next-token predictor trained on a much larger corpus that includes Cowen alongside millions of other writers. But the *style* of the model's outputs — particularly when prompted on the kinds of questions Cowen would address — has structural fingerprints of Cowen's voice. The model has absorbed the moves: the comparative angle, the unexpected reference, the willingness to take a position quickly, the slight asymmetry between the question being asked and the question the model chooses to answer.

Wang noticed this. And once he noticed it, he started using the model the way he uses Tyler.

## The Substitution Move

The mechanics of the substitution are simple enough to describe but interesting enough to be worth slowing down on.

Wang has built, over years of friendship and mentorship, a *cognitive habit* around Tyler-conversations. He thinks of questions in a particular way because he is anticipating what Tyler would do with them. He keeps the running list. He prepares some context. He shows up ready to spar — to push back, to extend, to reorient the question if Tyler's reaction reveals it was the wrong question.

ChatGPT doesn't have Tyler's actual mind. It has, at best, the Tyler-flavored layer of its training. But for the purposes of Wang's specific cognitive practice — *get a Tyler-like reaction so I can spar with it* — the layer is sufficient. *If I really wanted to have an instant Tyler-like reaction to a novel that I've just read or a piece of music that I've just heard, I just ask ChatGPT, and it is able to give me some really good answers.*[^1] The model produces a reaction that triggers the same mental sparring move Wang would have made with Tyler in person. Wang's cognition continues from there: he pushes back, extends, adjusts. The model, like Tyler in person, gives him something to *think against*.

The substitution is incomplete in important ways. Tyler-the-person remembers earlier conversations; the model does not (within a session) and even with memory features cannot reconstruct the depth of accumulated context Tyler has on Wang specifically. Tyler-the-person can introduce Wang to other people, push him into specific writing opportunities, model intellectual virtues over a multi-year arc. The model does none of this. The substitution captures one particular feature of Tyler — *generalist sparring reactions in real-time* — and substitutes a much weaker version of Tyler in all the other dimensions, mostly absent.

But for the use case Wang is describing — *I just read Stendhal, I want a smart reaction so my own thinking can sharpen against it; I just heard Mahler, I want a musicological gloss so I can extend my own reaction* — the substitution works. The model is not Tyler. It is a *Tyler-like creature*, available at any time, infinitely patient, free at the margin. Wang treats it as such.

## The Spanish Inquisition Question

The example Wang gives of his first really good ChatGPT experience is a small one but it captures the texture of the practice.

*Why did the Spanish Catholic Church develop such a virulent inquisition whereas the Austrian Catholics had no inquisition?*[^1]

The question itself is the kind Wang would have asked Tyler. It is comparative. It pulls together two things normally treated separately (Spanish Catholicism, Austrian Catholicism) and asks for a structural account of their divergence. It is not a question with a quick Wikipedia answer; it requires synthesizing across history, theology, political economy, ethnology. It is a question whose value is partly in *the texture of a good answer* — what considerations the answerer brings forward, which factors they weight, what comparative cases they invoke.

Wang has the question because he has spent time in both Catholic worlds and felt the difference. *Spanish Catholicism feels gloomy and slightly violent and a little bit dark; Austrian Catholicism feels bright, joyful, resplendent, much more crimson rather than very black.*[^1] The question is not abstract. It has been generated by Wang's own observational experience of two religious cultures and the felt-sense that the difference must be explainable.

He asked the model. The model produced an answer that *felt right*.[^1] We do not get the answer in the transcript — the relevant point is not what the model said but that the conversation succeeded as the kind of intellectual exchange Wang had previously been having with Tyler. The model produced a structural account that addressed the question on its own terms, mobilized appropriate comparative material, and gave Wang something to push against.

The Spanish-vs-Austrian question is the canonical instance of what the AI-as-Tyler-substitute can do well. Comparative, structural, requiring generalist synthesis, not requiring deep specialist accuracy. The model excels at exactly this register. It is less reliable on questions that require precise factual recall (where hallucinations bite) or on questions that require deep specialist judgment (where the model averages across sources rather than reasoning from expertise). The Tyler-substitute use case is in the *middle layer* — questions that benefit from broad intellectual range and structural thinking, without requiring expertise that exceeds what the model can plausibly synthesize.

## The Sparring Architecture

Perell's framing of what Wang is describing is worth dwelling on. Most users approach AI by asking it for *answers*. Wang approaches AI by asking it for *reactions to push against*. The reframing changes the cognitive role of the AI.

In the answer-mode, the AI's output is the destination. The user receives the output, accepts or rejects it, moves on. The user's cognitive activity is filtering rather than producing.

In the sparring-mode, the AI's output is the *instigator*. The user has a half-formed question or hypothesis. The AI produces a response that triggers the user's own cognitive engagement — agreement that extends the thinking, disagreement that sharpens it, partial acceptance that splits the question into newer questions. The user's cognitive activity is producing rather than filtering.

The sparring architecture is what Wang has imported from his Tyler-relationship into his AI use. *That's the process of thinking through things. That's the process of trying to figure out what are the right questions and what is the right approach, what is the right observational style.*[^1] The AI is not telling Wang what to think. It is providing a *worthy interlocutor* whose responses are good enough that Wang's own thinking is sharpened by reacting to them.

The architecture has a subtle prerequisite. The user has to already *have* something to spar with. The hypothesis, the half-formed observation, the question generated by their own engagement with material the AI has not seen. Without that input, the user is just asking the AI for an answer, and the AI produces an answer, and the cognitive engagement is the answer-mode rather than the sparring-mode. The sparring requires the user to *bring something* to the conversation, and the more interesting the user brings, the more useful the model's reaction becomes.

## What This Implies for AI Practice

The Tyler-substitute framework converts cleanly into a practice principle. *Use AI for the generalist-reaction function, in conversations you initiate with material you have already engaged with.* The good prompts in this register are not *teach me X* but *I have been thinking about X, and here is what I noticed, what would you say back?* The model becomes useful not as an oracle but as an interlocutor. The user's pre-existing engagement is what the model's reaction can sharpen.

The framework also implies that AI use has a *generalist substitute layer* and a *specialist substitute layer*, and they should be evaluated differently. For generalist sparring (comparative history, music, art, philosophy, structural analysis), the model is genuinely useful and the Tyler-substitute mode applies. For specialist work (technical implementation, primary-source research, expert judgment in domains where the model averages across mediocre sources), the model is much less useful and the user should not be using it the same way. Confusing the two layers — using the model for specialist work in the generalist mode — is where the hallucination problems and the bad-citation problems concentrate.

## Evidence

[^1] Wang's account of the Tyler-substitute use of AI runs from lines 444-462 of the transcript. Specific claims and locations: "Tyler Cowan thought has influenced a lot of how ChatGPT communicates" + "on the record, kind of established" (line 446); "the way that I treat ChatGPT is as my friend Tyler, who I maybe see once every couple of months in DC or in New York" (line 448); "instant Tyler-like reaction to a novel that I've just read or a piece of music that I've just heard" (line 450); running list of questions for Tyler in notes (line 452); Spanish vs Austrian Catholic Inquisition question + Spanish "gloomy slightly violent dark" vs Austrian "bright joyful resplendent crimson" + first really good ChatGPT experience (lines 456-460); "Tyler-like creature in my pocket" (line 460); "process of thinking through things... finding the right questions, right approach, right observational style" (line 462); reaffirmation of the verboten on flat sentences in writing (line 462).

## Tensions

The framework has tensions with both the AI-skeptic and AI-optimist positions.

Against the *AI-skeptic* position that LLMs cannot produce useful intellectual exchange because they are stochastic parrots without understanding, Wang's framework offers a counter-example. The Tyler-substitute use of AI is, by Wang's account, genuinely cognitively productive — it produces the same kind of thinking-sharpening that human conversation with a generalist intellectual produces. The skeptic position has to either dismiss Wang's experience as illusion or concede that, at the level of cognitive function rather than ontology, the model is doing something useful regardless of whether it "understands."

Against the *AI-optimist* position that LLMs can replace human intellectual exchange entirely, Wang's framework also offers a check. The Tyler-substitute is *for specific use cases* — generalist sparring on material the user has already engaged with. The model is *not* a substitute for the long-arc relationship Wang has with Tyler-the-person, for the deep specialist work Wang does on China, or for the writing that constitutes Wang's voice. The optimist position has to recognize that the AI-as-intellectual-companion role is genuine but bounded.

The harder tension is over the *Tyler-influence* claim itself. The empirical fact that Cowen's writing has influenced ChatGPT is plausible (Cowen is widely read and represented in training corpora) but also somewhat anecdotal and unverified at the precise level Wang is claiming. The vault should hold this as Wang's reading rather than as an empirical fact, and remain open to the possibility that the *Tyler-flavor* Wang detects is partly a function of Wang's expectations and partly a function of the model's training rather than a clean attribution.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The framework converges with Wang's own [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/ai-as-consumption-enhancer-not-writing-tool|AI as Consumption Enhancer, Not Writing Tool]] page (the companion concept). Both pages are products of Wang's overall AI framework: AI is excellent at the *layer wrapped around the user's experience* (consumption-enhancement, generalist-sparring) and verboten at the *layer that constitutes the user's cognitive output* (sentence-generation, voice). The two pages should be read together as the two sides of Wang's framework.

The framework also tensions with the broader AI-collaboration corpus in the vault. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/beta-editor-review-skill|Beta Editor Review Skill]] and adjacent pages treat AI as a simulated audience or wind-tunnel for testing one's own ideas. Wang's Tyler-substitute framing is similar but more specific — the AI is not a generic audience but a specifically-flavored interlocutor whose particular intellectual disposition (generalist, comparative, willing to take a position) makes it useful in a way a generic-audience framing does not capture. The convergence is on the underlying claim that AI is a thinking-partner; the divergence is in how specifically the partner can be characterized. Wang's framing implies that AI-as-thinking-partner is most useful when the user has a specific, characterized interlocutor model in mind, not when they are using the AI as a generic foil.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The Tyler-substitute framework reaches into psychology (the cognitive function of having a sparring partner), creative practice (the role of intellectual exchange in producing original work), and behavioral mechanics (the specific architecture of what makes a conversation productive).

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/identity-architecture-and-defense-hub|Identity Architecture and Defense Hub]] — the importance of *trusted interlocutors* in the development of mature thinking is well-documented in developmental psychology. Adolescents and young adults develop intellectual identity partly through extended sparring with a few mentors whose perspectives they argue with, internalize, and eventually push beyond. The handshake reveals that AI-as-Tyler-substitute is operating in the same psychological space — the user is engaging with a characterized interlocutor whose responses sharpen their own thinking — but with two important differences: the interlocutor is not real (which may matter for identity formation in ways the framework does not address) and the interlocutor is infinitely patient (which removes the social stakes that sometimes make human sparring more cognitively engaging). The implication: AI-substitute interlocutors may be useful for thinking-sharpening but may be inadequate substitutes for human mentors in identity-formation work, and the user should know which function they are using AI for.

- **Creative Practice**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/voice-cultivation-through-stylistic-models|Voice Cultivation Through Stylistic Models]] — the Tyler-substitute is, in a sense, a way of importing Cowen's stylistic intuitions into the user's own thinking process via the AI's training-influenced outputs. The handshake reveals a non-obvious symmetry: the writer who deliberately copies New Yorker articles and the user who deliberately uses ChatGPT-as-Tyler-substitute are doing structurally similar things — exposing themselves to a particular intellectual style in order to absorb its operations into their own thinking. The difference is the medium (handwritten/typed reproduction vs. AI conversation) and the granularity (sentence-level for copying, prompt-response-level for AI). Both are *deliberate exposure to a style* with the goal of cognitive transformation. Both are subject to the same caveat: choose your sources strategically, because the style you absorb shapes the thinking you become capable of.

- **Behavioral-Mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/behavioral-mechanics-hub|Behavioral Mechanics Hub]] (specifically pages on questioning techniques and elicitation) — the sparring architecture Wang describes is structurally similar to behavioral-mechanics protocols for generative questioning. The questioner brings specific material; the responder produces a reaction; the questioner pushes back; the productive thinking happens in the back-and-forth rather than in either side's individual contribution. The handshake produces an actionable claim: users who want to extract maximum value from AI conversation should approach it as a behavioral-mechanics protocol — bring specific input, ask for specific reactions rather than open-ended assistance, push back on the AI's responses rather than accepting them, iterate until the conversation produces something the user could not have produced alone. This is a learnable skill, not a default behavior, and most AI users are not yet practicing it.

- **Eastern Spirituality**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/sadhana-practice-hub|Sadhana Practice Hub]] — the running-list-of-questions practice Wang describes (questions for Tyler accumulated in his notes app, then unloaded when they meet) has a structural cousin in the spiritual practice of *holding questions for the next encounter with one's teacher*. In both cases, the questioner accumulates questions over time, lets them ripen, and presents them when the encounter happens. The handshake reveals that the practice is not about the immediate availability of the answer; it is about the *discipline of articulating the question well enough that it survives the wait*. The questions that survive accumulation and articulation tend to be better questions than the questions that get asked impulsively in the moment of confusion. The implication for AI use: even though the AI is always available, users may benefit from imposing artificial accumulation — keep questions for the AI in a running list, let them ripen, ask in batches rather than as they arrive — because the discipline produces better questions and better cognitive value from the eventual conversations.

The four handshakes converge on a single claim: *AI-as-sparring-partner is one specific application of a much broader principle about how thinking is sharpened through structured exchange with a characterized interlocutor*, and the value of the practice depends on the user's discipline in bringing material, characterizing the interlocutor, and treating the exchange as iterative rather than transactional.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

If the Tyler-substitute framework is correct, then the public conversation about AI's intellectual role is operating at the wrong level of generality. The question is not *can AI replace human intellectual exchange* (the answer is partly yes, partly no, depending on which functions of intellectual exchange you mean). The question is *which specific intellectual functions can which specific kinds of AI substitute for, and how much of the user's existing cognitive infrastructure does each substitution require*. Wang's case shows that AI can substitute for a specific friend's specific function (generalist sparring on material Wang has engaged with) for a user with specific cognitive infrastructure (an analytical writer with a pre-existing relationship to the friend). The substitution does not generalize: AI cannot substitute for the friend's other functions (mentorship, introductions, identity-formation) and cannot substitute for any function for users who lack the relevant cognitive infrastructure. The implication for AI policy and pedagogy is that the right questions are *narrow and specific*, not *broad and abstract*. Public conversation that treats AI's intellectual role as a single thing — *AI is good for thinking* or *AI cannot really think* — is missing the actual differentiation that determines whether any specific use produces cognitive enrichment or impoverishment.

**Generative Questions**
- Could a user deliberately *cultivate* AI-substitute relationships for multiple specific intellectual styles? Wang has Tyler. Could the same user develop their AI use to substitute for Cowen-on-economics, Hitchens-on-rhetoric, Eliot-on-poetry, and so on, by recognizing the trained-in stylistic fingerprints of different authors and prompting accordingly?
- Wang's running-list practice was developed for human friends and ported to AI. Are there other human-relationship cognitive practices that would port well to AI use, and which ones port badly?
- The *Tyler-influence* claim is interesting because it implies AI's outputs are *characterized* in ways most users may not recognize. If trained-in stylistic fingerprints are real, are users systematically being shaped by the styles their AI-of-choice reflects, in ways that average toward whichever writers are most heavily represented in training corpora? Is there a quiet homogenization happening at scale?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/ai-as-consumption-enhancer-not-writing-tool|AI as Consumption Enhancer, Not Writing Tool]] — companion concept; Wang's framework's other side
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/beta-editor-review-skill|Beta Editor Review Skill]] — adjacent AI-as-interlocutor framing
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/voice-cultivation-through-stylistic-models|Voice Cultivation Through Stylistic Models]] — structural cousin in the creative-practice domain
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/manuscript-copying-as-voice-training|Manuscript Copying as Voice Training]] — embodied analog of the same exposure mechanism
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/transformer-architecture-and-language-model-mechanics|Transformer Architecture and Language Model Mechanics]] — the technical layer that explains why training-corpus stylistic fingerprints exist

## Open Questions

- What is the actual evidence for the Cowen-influence-on-ChatGPT claim? Is this established in any documentable way, or is it widely-asserted-but-unverified? Wang treats it as common knowledge but the original citation is unclear.
- The Tyler-substitute framework requires the user to already have a relationship with a Tyler. Is the framework usable by users who don't have a Tyler — and if so, can they characterize the AI's interlocutor role through other means (specifying author personas in prompts, etc.)?
- Wang sees Tyler in person every few months. As AI conversation becomes default, does the value of in-person Tyler-equivalent relationships rise or fall? Are people who have access to both AI substitutes and human intellectual mentors at an advantage that compounds, or does AI substitution erode the human relationships over time?

## Cross-Source: Karlsson — AI as Targeted-Craft-Tool, Not Interlocutor (2026-05-12)

Henrik Karlsson adds a third position to this page's framing of AI use, structurally distinct from Wang's two frames (Cowen-substitute sparring partner; consumption-enhancer for reading). Karlsson uses AI for *targeted craft-mechanical tasks* — vocabulary lookup, grammar verification, sentence-variation generation, and bad-habits monitoring — comprising about 1% of his published words.[^2]

The four micro-uses Karlsson articulates:

**1. Lexical lookup for second-language gaps.** As a non-native English speaker, Karlsson uses the model as a thesaurus-on-demand: describe the meaning, get the candidate word. *"I might do things like — because I'm a second language, I don't know English all that well. Sometimes I'll describe a word and they'll give me the word because I don't know it."*[^2]

**2. Grammar verification.** Sanity-check on uncertain constructions. *"Or I'll ask, 'Is this grammatical?' or whatever."*[^2]

**3. Sentence-variation generation.** When stuck on a phrasing: *"Sometimes I'm not happy with a way something is phrased and I'll be like, 'Give me 10 versions of this with different words to just get me out of my head and see different possibilities.'"*[^2] The model is not asked to pick a version — it's asked to display a range, which the writer then selects from or uses as a launchpad.

**4. Bad-habits monitoring.** Karlsson stores his known writing-flaws in a prompt and has the model flag them during edit. *"I have a prompt where I ask it to go through, 'These are some words I overuse, can you point out when I use them?' These are other things I want to think about, just to help it remind me so I don't have to keep all the things I should look out for in my head."*[^2] The model offloads vigilance.

The Karlsson framing differs from Wang's Cowen-substitute frame in a structural way. Wang uses AI as *interlocutor* — conversational partner for thinking-through-problems, with characterized intellectual style influencing the exchange. Karlsson uses AI as *tool* — discrete craft-mechanical tasks with no expectation of intellectual exchange. The model is not Karlsson's thinking partner; it's his lookup, his variation engine, his vigilance store.

Karlsson is also a *power user* of LLMs — pre-ChatGPT access (special OpenAI beta from 2021), deep technical familiarity. His position is not knee-jerk avoidance. He's enthusiastic about the technology while specifically routing around it for substantive writing-work. *"I've been somewhat underwhelmed in what they've delivered so far. I've seen interesting images, interesting music, but I've not yet seen any good literature be made. They are incredible tools for research."*[^2]

The third-position-frame this opens: AI can be used at multiple resolutions of *substance*, and the appropriate use depends on the user's writing-practice.

- **Wang #1 (Cowen-substitute / interlocutor)**: AI for thinking-with at conversational scale. Useful for analytical writers who want characterized sparring partners.
- **Wang #2 (consumption-enhancer / reading tool)**: AI for ingesting and processing source material. Useful for writers in research-intensive practices.
- **Karlsson #3 (targeted-craft-tool / micro-mechanic)**: AI for discrete word/grammar/variation/edit tasks. Useful for writers whose substantive work happens outside the tool.

Karlsson also articulates a deeper concern this page hasn't addressed: **LLMs as standardization-pressure on the prose-field**. He argues that even non-LLM-using writers face ambient smoothing-pressure as LLM-edited text circulates more widely. The defense, in his framing, is to be *wilder with grammar* — deliberately import constructions from other languages (Turkish, Persian, Swedish) to maintain distance from the statistical center the models pull toward. *"LLMs are just another force for standardization. If English is poised to become the global language, we should make an effort to bring in all the weird innovations from all the other languages."*[^2] This is a structural-ecology claim, not a personal-use claim — and it adds a layer to the business framework neither Wang frame addresses.

The full three-frame picture: Wang's two frames optimize for *what AI does well* (interlocutor; consumption-helper); Karlsson's frame optimizes for *minimal AI presence in production* combined with *defensive practice against ambient standardization*. All three positions are coherent. They suit different writers and different writing-philosophies. The implication for this page: AI-as-Cowen-substitute is one of *several legitimate counter-positions* to mainstream AI-as-creative-collaborator framing, and the full counter-framework needs all three to be complete.

See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/llm-as-standardization-pressure-grammar-wildness-defense|LLM as Standardization Pressure — Grammar Wildness as Defense]] for the full Karlsson treatment.

## Footnotes

[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/henrik-karlsson-perell-interview|Karlsson, David Perell interview]] — transcript, [PARAPHRASED]; LLM use specifics (lexical lookup, grammar verification, sentence-variation, bad-habits prompt) at lines 372-380; "very little of what I put in the essays has been touched by LLMs" / 1% figure at line 374; power-user pre-ChatGPT background at lines 374-376; underwhelment with LLM literature at lines 376-378; standardization-pressure / grammar-wildness defense at lines 358-368.

# Allow for Serendipity

## The Idea That Arrives While You're Doing Something Else

Some of your best ideas didn't show up while you were staring hard at the problem. They showed up in the shower, half-asleep, on a walk, mid-conversation about something unrelated. You weren't trying. That's not a coincidence worth shrugging off — it's a pattern with a mechanism behind it, and Greene's second creative strategy is built on learning to invite it deliberately instead of waiting for it to happen by accident.

## What Narrow Focus Actually Costs

Your brain runs as a dual processing system — every piece of incoming information gets compared, in real time, against everything else it's already holding, hunting for similarities, differences, and relationships. That comparison engine is where new associations come from.[^1]

Here's the problem. When you're deep in a project, concentrating hard, attention narrows and tension rises — and the brain responds by cutting down the amount of incoming stimuli it processes, specifically so it can focus on what feels necessary. That narrowing makes you more effective at the immediate task and worse at noticing anything adjacent to it. Relax that focus, and attention widens back out, taking in more of what's actually around you.[^2] Serendipity — the useful thing you weren't looking for — needs the wide state to have any chance of registering at all.

## Two Deliberate Steps

Greene turns this into a two-part practice, since chance itself can't be forced, only invited.

**Step one: widen the search further than feels efficient.** In the research phase of a project, look at more than what's strictly required. Pull in adjacent fields. If you're testing a theory, chase down more examples and potential counterexamples than seems reasonable. William James described the resulting mental state vividly — the mind moving between ideas, "the most unheard of combination of elements," a seething cauldron where everything is "fizzling and bobbling about." That excess of stimulation builds a kind of momentum, where the smallest chance occurrence can spark something real.[^3]

**Step two: maintain looseness, deliberately, in the middle of the work.** Take walks. Do something unrelated (Einstein played the violin). And crucially: when something unexpected shows up in your mind, don't dismiss it just because it seems irrational or doesn't fit the frame of your current project. Give it real attention and see where it actually leads before deciding it's noise.[^4]

## Analytical Case Study: The Chickens That Wouldn't Die

Louis Pasteur's germ theory work put him deep into medicine and chemistry, chasing the idea that specific microorganisms caused specific diseases — a genuinely novel claim at the time.

In 1879, he had cultures of chicken cholera prepared, then got pulled onto other projects, and the cultures sat untouched in his lab for months. When he finally returned to them, he injected them into chickens expecting the usual result. Instead, every chicken recovered easily. His working assumption was that time had weakened the cultures, so he ordered fresh ones and injected them into both the previously exposed chickens and a new batch. The new chickens died as expected. Every one of the old chickens survived.[^5]

Other doctors before Pasteur had likely seen something similar and let it pass — an anomaly not worth pursuing. Pasteur's years of accumulated knowledge in the field meant he immediately recognized what he was looking at: the aged cultures had weakened enough to trigger immunity without triggering illness. That single observation cracked open the entire practice of inoculation — protecting the body by deliberately exposing it to a weakened form of a disease.[^6] His own phrase for the underlying condition that made this possible: "Chance favors only the prepared mind."[^7]

## Analytical Case Study: The Sound He Was Trying to Kill

Thomas Edison's version runs on the same mechanism from a completely different field. He was deep in an unglamorous engineering problem — improving how paper moved through a telegraph machine, recording dots and dashes — and the thing driving him crazy was a specific noise the mechanism made: "a light, musical, rhythmical sound, resembling human talk heard indistinctly."[^8]

He set the telegraph project aside for months, but the sound kept haunting him. One day, hearing it again in his head, an idea landed that had nothing to do with telegraphs: what if this mechanism could be adapted to record sound and the human voice directly? Months of immersing himself in the science of acoustics followed, using technology close to what he already understood from telegraphy — and the first experimental phonograph came out the other end.[^9]

Greene's point in pairing these cases: nobody could have reasoned their way to the phonograph by deliberately imagining paper rolls that record sound. That specific connection required an accident — a whirring noise that refused to be ignored — landing on a mind that had already spent months in exactly the adjacent technical territory needed to interpret it.[^10]

## Why It Isn't Only a Science Trick

The chance-plus-preparation mechanism generalizes past laboratories. Writer Anthony Burgess, stuck in stale patterns, sometimes picked random words from a reference book and let their order dictate a novel's plot — pure chance as a starting point, worked afterward into a fully crafted structure by his conscious mind. Surrealist Max Ernst made prints from the accidental grooves of an overscrubbed wood floor, then built hallucinatory drawings out of what the prints suggested.[^11] Neither artist was outsourcing the work to randomness. Both were using deliberately introduced chance to break a stuck pattern, then applying real craft to what the chance turned up.

Two closely related practices deserve their own separate treatment rather than a passing mention here: keeping a notebook to catch ideas at the exact moment they arrive (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-notebook-practice|The Notebook Practice]]), and training yourself to think in deliberate analogies rather than waiting for chance associations alone (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/analogical-thinking|Analogical Thinking]]). Both are Greene's own direct extensions of the serendipity strategy, distinct enough in mechanism and evidence to earn their own pages.

## What "Prepared" Actually Means Here

Pasteur's own phrase — "chance favors only the prepared mind" — is easy to nod along with and easy to misapply, because "prepared" doesn't mean generically smart or generically well-read. It means holding enough specific depth in the exact area the chance encounter touches that the mind can recognize significance the instant it appears, rather than needing to research it first. Pasteur wasn't prepared for chicken cholera in general — he was prepared for *exactly that* anomaly, by years of prior work in the same narrow territory. Serendipity, in other words, still rewards depth. It just rewards depth combined with looseness, not depth alone.

## Implementation Workflow

You're deep in a project and stuck. Resist the instinct to narrow further, digging harder into the same material. Widen instead — read something adjacent, unrelated, even irrelevant-seeming. The stuckness is often the narrowed-attention state doing exactly what it's built to do: filtering out the very stimulus that would unstick you.

Something odd or irritating keeps recurring while you work on something else entirely — a sound, a phrase, a small recurring annoyance. Don't dismiss it as background noise. Edison's phonograph came from refusing to let an annoying sound stay unexamined.

You get an idea that seems to have nothing to do with your actual project. Give it real attention before discarding it. The test isn't whether it fits your current frame — it's whether, examined honestly, it actually leads somewhere.

You notice an experimental result, or a small real-world event, that doesn't match what you expected. Before explaining it away, ask what you'd have to believe for it to be meaningful rather than noise. Pasteur's whole discovery sat inside an assumption — "the cultures just weakened" — that turned out to be exactly wrong in the most useful possible way.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

Pasteur's chicken cholera discovery and Edison's phonograph development are both standard, well-documented history-of-science cases, and Greene's account tracks the record closely.

**The dual-processing brain claim is stated with more neuroscientific confidence than the underlying research supports.** "The brain operates as a dual processing system" is asserted flatly, without citation, in a book aimed at a popular audience — this is closer to a useful working metaphor for association-formation than a precise account of how attention and memory actually interact at the neural level. Treat the mechanism description as heuristic, not settled science. `[CONTESTED]`

**Survivorship bias runs through every case here.** Pasteur and Edison had a lifetime of preparation behind the chance moment that paid off. Greene doesn't address how many equally prepared minds had equally strange chance encounters that led nowhere — the strategy's actual hit rate, even for well-prepared people, is invisible in a book built entirely from success stories.

**Open question:** the strategy requires both wide search *and* narrow enough prior expertise to recognize when something chance-encountered actually matters. How does a relative beginner — without Pasteur's or Edison's years of accumulated pattern-recognition — tell a genuine serendipitous opening from ordinary noise?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

This strategy sits in real tension with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/cultivate-negative-capability|Cultivate Negative Capability]], the strategy immediately preceding it in the same chapter. Negative Capability asks for sustained, effortful attention held on a single unresolved question. Serendipity asks for exactly the opposite — relaxed, widened attention, deliberately *not* focused on the problem. Greene presents both as necessary without reconciling the apparent contradiction: how does a practitioner know, in a given work session, whether to bear down (Negative Capability) or loosen up (Serendipity)? The honest reading is that they're sequential phases within the same larger process, not simultaneous postures — but Greene never states the sequencing rule explicitly.

There's a convergence worth naming with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/the-fact-of-great-yield|The Fact of Great Yield]], built later in this same chapter from Ramachandran's career. Both pages describe a prepared mind encountering an anomaly and recognizing significance where others see only noise — Pasteur's chickens and Ramachandran's phantom-limb anomalies are structurally the same event. The difference is emphasis: Serendipity treats the anomaly as arriving by pure accident; Great Yield treats actively hunting for anomalies as the deliberate professional discipline. Together they suggest the real skill isn't choosing between chance and search — it's building enough prepared attention that chance and deliberate search start producing the same kind of catch.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/paul-graham-and-the-social-reversal|Paul Graham and the Social Reversal]]** — Y Combinator's founding insight, as told in that page, was itself a serendipitous encounter: Graham's dislike of Windows programming led him toward a web-application architecture nobody had built for that purpose, discovered essentially by accident while trying to avoid an unrelated annoyance. The insight the pairing produces: serendipity in Greene's corpus isn't confined to science and art — it's the same mechanism generating major business models, and the "prepared mind" in Graham's case was years of hacker culture and a stated aesthetic aversion, not formal business training. The preparation that pays off doesn't have to look like domain expertise from the outside.

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-path-of-no-path-effortless-effort|The Path of No Path — Effortless Effort]]** names the same structural paradox from inside contemplative practice: how do you make a deliberate effort toward a recognition that only arrives once effort stops? Serendipity's second step — deliberately loosening grip, allowing rather than forcing an association — is a secular, professional-output-flavored version of exactly that paradox. The insight the pairing produces: both traditions independently concluded that direct pursuit of the target state can block the target state, and both resolve it the same way — not by abandoning effort, but by redirecting effort toward the *conditions* that make the ungrippable thing more likely to arrive (widened search, sustained practice) rather than gripping at the thing itself. Neither tradition names the other, but they've converged on an identical structural fix.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** If narrow focus mechanically suppresses the stimuli that produce serendipity, then the popular advice to "just work harder" on a stuck problem may be actively counterproductive at exactly the moment it's most often given. The discomfort of being stuck is frequently the signal to relax attention, not intensify it — which runs directly against the instinct most people have when a deadline looms.

**Generative questions.**
- If serendipity requires both wide search and narrowed prior expertise, is there a way to accelerate the "prepared mind" half for someone working outside their primary field, where accidental competence hasn't yet accumulated?
- Pasteur and Edison both recognized their anomalies within the same field they were already working in. What happens when the anomaly that matters shows up in a field the practitioner has no expertise in at all?
- Greene frames serendipity as something you "allow" rather than force. Is there a meaningful upper limit to how much of it can be systematically engineered — through deliberate practices like widened reading and notebook-keeping — before it stops being chance and just becomes a slower, more roundabout form of directed search?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-dimensional-mind|The Dimensional Mind]] — the framework this strategy serves
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/cultivate-negative-capability|Cultivate Negative Capability]] — the preceding strategy, in tension over focus versus looseness
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-notebook-practice|The Notebook Practice]] — the tool for catching serendipitous ideas at the moment they arrive
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/analogical-thinking|Analogical Thinking]] — the deliberate counterpart to chance association
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/the-fact-of-great-yield|The Fact of Great Yield]] — Ramachandran's version of the prepared mind meeting an anomaly
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/paul-graham-and-the-social-reversal|Paul Graham and the Social Reversal]] — serendipity producing a business model rather than a scientific discovery

# People Are Contradictory: Philadelphia Story / Walkabout (Hari)

## "The Time to Make Your Mind Up About Someone Is Never"

Hari quotes a line from the 1940 film *The Philadelphia Story* that he calls one of his favorites: *"the time to make your mind up about someone is never."*[^1] Then he gives the evidence. He's interviewed people who've done terrible things and one incredibly good thing in their lives. He's interviewed people who were wonderful and then catastrophically destructive. People are everywhere in between. When you're telling a story about someone, the temptation is to *act like you've captured their essence.* People don't have essences. They have multitudes — Whitman's word, used by Hari directly.

The corollary is craft-operational. The writer who goes in looking for *the one thing that unlocks the subject* is going in with the wrong tool. There is no one thing. The honest portrait gives the reader the *space to be complex, contradictory, ambiguous.* If the writer collapses the multitude into a single trait, the portrait flattens — and the flatness is what makes the work feel manipulative even when the writer didn't intend to manipulate.

## What This Actually Is

Hari is making a structural claim about how *truthful portrayal of human beings* works. The claim has three load-bearing parts.

**Part 1 (ontological):** Humans don't have essences. The notion of a person's *single underlying truth* is an artifact of bad biography, not a description of how persons actually exist. Persons exist as bundles of behaviors, traits, contradictions, history-marks. The bundles cohere enough to be recognized as *the same person across time*, but they don't reduce to a single underlying trait.

**Part 2 (craft):** Treating subjects as having an essence flattens them in the writing. The flat portrait is what produces the readerly experience of *being preached to* — the writer has already collapsed the subject into a moral judgment, and the reader has to accept or reject the judgment without being given the material to think with. The complex portrait produces the readerly experience of *thinking with the writer* — the contradictions are visible, the judgment is partial, the reader has work to do.

**Part 3 (ethical):** Subjects deserve the dignity of being represented as complex. This applies *symmetrically* — to subjects the writer likes and subjects the writer doesn't like. The temptation in both directions is the same: the writer wants their hero to be a hero and their villain to be a villain. Both temptations betray the actual people. *"Demonization and valorization are equally untruthful."*

## The Walkabout / Pauline Kael Principle

Hari illustrates with a Pauline Kael review of the Australian film *Walkabout* (the 1971 Nicolas Roeg film about two white children rescued in the desert by a young Aboriginal boy). Kael argued that the film *represents the Aboriginal characters as kind of magical and mystical, and what it denies them is the dignity of just being real people like everyone else.*[^1]

Hari adopts the principle. *Demonization and valorization are equally untruthful or oversimplifications of human beings.* The film that turns its Aboriginal hero into a magical-mystical archetype hasn't honored him — it's flattened him in the opposite direction from a racist demonization, but the flattening is structurally the same. The mature portrayal gives the character the dignity of being a *real person* — flawed, particular, with the same range of qualities the white characters get.

Hari applies the principle directly to the work he's currently doing. He's writing about homeless people in Las Vegas. They've been demonized — devils, dangers, blights. The temptation is to swing the other way: *no, they're angels, they're saints, they're the wisest people you'd ever meet.* That's not dignity. That's *valorization-as-equal-disrespect.* The actual person — like Tommy, the homeless friend Hari mentions, who was murdered — was someone who *had complicated qualities, did some absolutely remarkable things, and did some bad things.* The portrait must hold all of it. The flattening in either direction would betray him.

## Synergies & Handshakes

This page is the worldview-corollary of [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/look-for-reason-to-love-them-interview-stance-hari|Look for a Reason to Love Them (Hari)]] and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/i-dont-believe-in-evil-only-evil-acts-arpaio-hari|"I Don't Believe in Evil" (Hari)]]. The three pages form a unit: the stance produces openness, the openness produces foundational stories, and the foundational stories reveal the people as multitudes rather than essences.

It connects strongly to [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/lieberman-mindreader-uncertainty-of-other-minds|Lieberman Mindreader: Uncertainty of Other Minds]] — Lieberman's central claim is that our reads of other people's minds are systematically more uncertain than we treat them. Hari's craft principle is the operational corollary: since reads are uncertain, portrayals should be *complex enough to honor the uncertainty*. The simple portrait pretends to a certainty the actual epistemics doesn't support.

It sits in productive tension with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/character-anchor-traits-bilton|Character-Anchor Traits (Bilton)]] — Bilton's craft method gives each character a *single distinctive trait* the reader can hold (Rubik's-cube-guy, fast-walker, slow-blinker). Hari warns against the single-trait approach for *real* people in nonfiction. The tension is productive because it points at a distinction the vault should hold: in fiction or narrative-condensation, single-trait anchors help readers track many characters; in deep portrayal of real subjects, single-trait anchors flatten the subject and produce manipulation. The same technique that helps thirty fictional characters cohere can destroy a single real subject's truthfulness. The vault holds both.

## Analytical Case Study: Tommy, the Homeless Friend

Hari mentions, in passing, someone he calls Tommy — a homeless man Hari had been writing about for years, who was murdered before the book about Vegas was finished. Hari describes the temptation he had to manage: the temptation to *sanitize* Tommy. Homeless people are demonized in contemporary American discourse. The natural counter-move is to swing them to the opposite pole — present Tommy as the saint of the underclass, the wise prophet of survival, the moral superior of the people who passed him on the street.

Hari refuses both poles. *Tommy was complicated and he had some absolutely remarkable qualities and one of the best people I've ever known and he did some bad things and it's tempting to downplay the bad things, but I have to say to myself, no, because that's not according him the dignity of being who he was.*[^1]

The bad things stay in the portrait. Not as moral lecture, not as gotcha — as part of the truthful complexity of who Tommy was. The remarkable qualities stay in the portrait. Not as sanctification — as part of the same complexity. The reader closes the chapter with a sense of *who Tommy was*, not as a category (homeless-saint or homeless-degenerate) but as a particular human being whose life resists summary.

This is the operational meaning of *dignity* in Hari's craft. Dignity is not flattery. Dignity is the refusal to flatten. The bad things are part of dignity precisely because honoring the person means honoring all of them.

## Implementation Workflow: The Mid-Manuscript Audit

You're three-quarters through the book. You print out the chapters that profile your main subjects. You sit with them at the kitchen table with a red pen.

For each subject, you ask three questions.

*First:* What's the one trait this portrait is using to anchor the subject? Find the sentences that do the anchoring work. Are there too few of them? Too many? Has the trait become the whole portrait?

*Second:* What's the opposite of that trait — what does this subject also do, also feel, also embody that *contradicts* the anchor trait? If you can't find the contradiction in your draft, you've flattened. The contradiction is in the subject. Your job is to surface it.

*Third:* What's the worst thing this subject has done? If the portrait is of someone you like (a hero of the project, a sympathetic witness), the question gets uncomfortable. Have you suppressed the worst thing? If you have, your portrayal isn't honoring them — it's valorizing them. Put the worst thing in. Not as gotcha, not as undermining the hero, but as the *texture of dignity*.

Conversely: if the portrait is of someone you dislike (a villain, an antagonist), what is the *unexpectedly good thing* they did? The thing that, when you found it, complicated your relationship to your own portrayal? If you can't find the good thing, you haven't done the work. The good thing is somewhere in their life. Your portrait isn't done until you've found it and let it stand alongside the bad.

You do this for every named subject. The portraits get harder, more uncomfortable, more *real*. The book gets better.

## The Single-Trait Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

You'll know the portrait has flattened when readers describe your subjects in a single sentence after closing the book. *"That was the chapter about the cruel sheriff."* *"That was the saint who lived under the bridge."* The single-sentence summary is the diagnostic — the reader has caught only the anchor and missed the multitude. Sometimes this is the right artistic choice (short profiles, character glimpses), but for sustained portrayal of major subjects it's the failure mode. The reader's takeaway should resist single-sentence summary.

You'll know it's working when readers describe your subjects as *complicated*. *"That sheriff — I don't know what to think about him."* *"Tommy — he was so much more than I expected him to be."* The complication is the work. The complication is what makes the portrayal honor the subject. The complication is also what makes the book hard to forget.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

Hari's claim has plenty of company. Orlean's portrait methods. Tracy Kidder's character work. Patrick Radden Keefe's complex sympathies. Jung on the integration of opposites within a single self. Tucker Max's same insistence on contradictory truthful portrayal. Five writers from five different rooms keep arriving at the same move because the move is what people actually are.

The open tension: short-form journalism (5,000-word features, op-eds) can't always afford the complex portrayal at full depth. The constraint produces a structural difficulty — short-form has to anchor with single traits to be readable in the word count, but the single-trait anchor is the failure mode Hari warns against. The likely resolution is that short-form pieces should *flag their own simplification* — admit to the reader that the portrait is partial — rather than implicitly claim completeness. Hari's longform books have room for the complexity. Short-form should claim less.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Hari and Greene are mutually corrective. Greene's *Laws of Human Nature* tends toward type-classification — narcissist, envious, gender-rigid, etc. The taxonomy gives the reader operational handles for recognizing dangerous patterns in other people. Hari's principle pushes back: the type-classification, taken too literally, produces the *demonization* Hari warns against. The corrective Hari offers Greene is *type as one face of a multitude, not the whole face.* The corrective Greene offers Hari is *some patterns are dangerous enough to need operational handles even at the cost of some flattening — the cost of recognizing a narcissist too late may be greater than the cost of flattening the portrayal in your head.* The vault should hold both correctives. They're appropriate at different stages of engagement: Greene's typing is useful at first encounter when you need to protect yourself; Hari's complexity is required for the deeper portrayal once protection isn't the primary concern.

Hari and Karlsson converge on the suspicion of essence. Karlsson treats writing as *discovery* — the writer doesn't know in advance what they're going to find, including about themselves. Hari treats subjects as *not-yet-knowable* — the writer doesn't know in advance who they are, including the most familiar subjects. Both writers reject the *I have already understood you/myself* posture as the entry to flattened work. The convergence reveals that *honest portrayal requires sustained uncertainty about the subject*, whether the subject is the writer (Karlsson) or the writer's interviewees (Hari).

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The multitudes principle shows up in two other domains worth naming.

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/integration-of-the-multitudes-jung-internal-family|Integration of the Multitudes: Jung / Internal Family Systems]] — Jungian and Internal Family Systems frameworks treat the individual as a cluster of part-selves that need integration, not as a unified essence to be discovered. The clinical insight is what Hari's craft principle says from outside. Single-essence portrayal of the self flattens the interior as much as it flattens the third-person portrait. The principle is symmetric across self-relation and other-relation. The writer who portrays others as multitudes — if they apply the principle inward — finds themselves to be multitudes too. This often is what produces the later-career shift toward more compassionate self-account that you see in mature memoirists.

- **Behavioral Mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/avoiding-fundamental-attribution-error|Avoiding Fundamental Attribution Error]] — Fundamental attribution error is the documented bias of attributing others' behavior to character while attributing your own to circumstance. Elite negotiators, investigators, and strategists deliberately counter the bias by holding their adversaries as situation-responding rather than essence-driven. Hari's craft discipline and the operator's strategic discipline are the same move. The writer who runs Hari's portrayal-discipline becomes a better strategic thinker almost as a side effect, because they've internalized the situation-over-essence read of other agents that the literature shows produces better predictions.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**
If Hari is right, the contemporary political ecosystem is structurally producing *demonization-or-valorization* portrayals of every public figure on every side, and the producer-incentives in the ecosystem reward flattening over complexity. The result is a public unable to think clearly about any of the actors in its own political life — they have only flattened images, and the flattened images can't support real understanding. The corollary: *political dysfunction is partly a flattening-of-portrayal dysfunction.* The journalism that would help — the complex portrayal of figures across the political spectrum — would also be the journalism that *underperforms commercially in the current incentive structure*. The structural problem is not that complex portrayals don't exist. It's that they're outcompeted by flattened ones. Restoring the public's capacity for political thought requires changing the incentives that select for flattening, which is not a writer-level intervention.

**Generative Questions**
- *Is the multitudes principle universally applicable?* Some figures (career-long perpetrators, organized criminals with documented patterns) may have *enough behavioral consistency* that the multitudes claim feels strained. Are there exceptions, or do even the most consistent perpetrators have unrecognized contradictions that honest portrayal would reveal?
- *Does writing complex portrayals require a kind of moral courage that's underdiscussed?* The reader who wants the demonization will be angry at the writer who refuses it. The reader who wants the valorization will be angry at the writer who refuses *that*. The complex portrayal alienates both flanks. The writer who runs Hari's method is choosing to be misread by activists on every side. What sustains the writer through that alienation?
- *Does the principle apply to historical figures we can't interview?* The biographer working from documents has less material than the journalist working with living subjects. Can the multitudes-portrayal be assembled from documents alone, or does it require some form of relational contact the documentary biographer doesn't have? MacCulloch's may-have-discipline suggests yes, but the operational specifics differ.

## Connected Concepts
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/look-for-reason-to-love-them-interview-stance-hari|Look for a Reason to Love Them (Hari)]] — the stance that produces the access to multitudes
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/i-dont-believe-in-evil-only-evil-acts-arpaio-hari|"I Don't Believe in Evil" (Hari)]] — the philosophical corollary
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/truthfully-complicated-stories-vs-nonfiction-trope-hari|Truthfully Complicated Stories vs Nonfiction Trope (Hari)]] — the narrative architecture downstream
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/character-anchor-traits-bilton|Character-Anchor Traits (Bilton)]] — the fiction-craft sibling-and-tension
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/may-have-discipline-degrees-of-confidence|"May Have" Discipline (MacCulloch)]] — the epistemic register for the same claim
